# Mutations

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A mutation makes snapshot-atomic logical reads, buffers writes, validates its
captured dependencies, and commits once. It does not hold one SQLite read
transaction across arbitrary asynchronous handler work; commit-time OCC rejects
relevant drift between reads. Every row changed by the commit receives the
same monotonic version. A rejected mutation commits nothing.

When one screen calls several of these mutations against the same resource id,
declare them once with `defineSurface` instead of rewiring each call site — see
[application surfaces](../clients/surfaces.md), which binds a resource's reads,
mutations, assets, and presence around shared parameters. The mutations
themselves are unchanged; a surface only composes the generated references.

## Define the write boundary

The paved JS form colocates its direct handler expression with arguments,
result contract, and possible writes:

```js source=demos/signal-desk/snapback/functions.mjs
export const createIncident = defineJsMutation({
  args: {
    title: v.string(),
    severity: v.string(),
    actorId: v.string(),
    now: v.integer(),
  },
  result: results.value(v.id('incidents')),
  writes: ['incidents', 'activity'],
  handler: async (ctx, args) => {
    const title = String(args.title ?? '').trim();
    if (!title) throw new Error('incident title is required');
    if (!new Set(['SEV-1', 'SEV-2', 'SEV-3']).has(args.severity)) {
      throw new Error('invalid severity');
    }
    const incidentId = await ctx.db.insert('incidents', {
      title,
      summary: 'Investigation started. Add tasks and field notes as evidence arrives.',
      severity: args.severity,
      status: 'investigating',
      commanderId: args.actorId,
      createdAt: args.now,
      updatedAt: args.now,
    });
    await ctx.db.insert('activity', {
      incidentId,
      actorId: args.actorId,
      sourceTable: 'incidents',
      sourceId: incidentId,
      operation: 'insert',
      effectiveSubject: args.actorId,
      actualActor: args.actorId,
      actorKind: 'human',
      mutationDigest: 'explicit-js-handler.v1',
      kind: 'incident.created',
      detail: `${args.severity} incident opened`,
      createdAt: args.now,
      sortKey: args.now,
    });
    return incidentId;
  },
});
```

Those two bare `throw`s are the minimum: they reject the write, but the caller
receives only a generic handler failure. As soon as a caller could *act* on
the reason — retry with a different value, be shown copy — declare the code
instead; see
[refuse with a declared code](#refuse-with-a-declared-code-not-a-bare-throw).

<!-- since: 0.1.16 -->

The hand-rolled severity domain guard above predates **stored enums**: a
field whose values come from a fixed set now declares that set on the schema
— `severity: v.union([v.literal('SEV-1'), v.literal('SEV-2'), v.literal('SEV-3')])`
— and every central writer then enforces the domain, refusing an
out-of-domain string with `SNAPBACK_FIELD_ENUM_VALUE_INVALID` (naming the
field and admitted values) and committing nothing. Declare the domain once
instead of re-checking it in every mutation; declaration rules and
narrowing semantics are
[closed string domains](../getting-started/your-first-backend.md#declare-the-schema).

The handler writes only through `ctx.db`. Server-owned ids, row versions, and
storage timestamps are never authored by the handler. An inline handler
captures no imports or top-level `const` bindings; statically reachable
same-file function declarations are resolved and spliced in with it. The legacy
`{ source, exportName }` form remains compatible but cannot be mixed with
`handler`; it also reads one closed script, supports same-file helpers, and
refuses imports with `BUNDLE_UNSUPPORTED_IMPORT`. Imported helpers, third-party
packages, and multi-file graphs are not admitted by that compatibility lane.

`defineMutation` is the declarative twin: compose `insert`, `patch`,
`delete`, conditions, and a declared return binding without running a JS
handler. The complete plan vocabulary — every step helper, the expression
algebra, return bindings, and the spec keys — is
[declarative mutation plans](./declarative-plans.md).

Strict `arg('name')` requires the property, so generation refuses a
caller-optional argument consumed by it with
`SNAPBACK_AUTHORING_OPTIONAL_ARG_CONTRADICTION`. Use `argOpt('name')` for the
omission branch: an omitted property evaluates to `null`; use
`coalesce(argOpt('name'), lit(default))` to supply a default. Writing that
`null` requires the target field to be declared `v.optional(...)`, which
stores it as a present null.

Set-oriented deletion is `deleteWhere(table, filter)`. The filter argument is
required; omitting it refuses generation with
`SNAPBACK_DELETE_WHERE_FILTER_REQUIRED`. An explicitly authored empty array,
`deleteWhere(table, [])`, retains the clear-table IR and therefore means
"delete every row" deliberately. Never derive or substitute that empty array
for an absent filter.

Two transactional effects beyond `ctx.db` writes commit or roll back with the
same mutation and have their own pages: a declared `sequences` counter
allocated through `ctx.sequence.allocate`
([sequences](./sequences.md)) and durable follow-up work enqueued through
`ctx.jobs.enqueue` ([one-off durable jobs](./jobs.md)).

<!-- since: 0.1.15 -->

## Derive a replay-stable effect key

When a mutation records an intent that an action or worker will deliver to an
external provider, derive the provider idempotency key from
`ctx.mutation.settlement()`. Write the intent and key inside the transaction;
perform the network I/O later, outside the mutation:

```js source=crates/snapback/tests/mutation_settlement_identity_v0.rs
  async recordEffectIntent(ctx) {
    var settlement = await ctx.mutation.settlement();
    var providerIdempotencyKey = settlement.settlementId === null
      ? null
      : 'notification:' + settlement.settlementId;
    await ctx.db.insert('entries', {
      marker: providerIdempotencyKey === null ? 'no-settlement-identity' : providerIdempotencyKey,
      clientMutationId: settlement.clientMutationId,
      settlementId: settlement.settlementId
    });
    return {
      queued: providerIdempotencyKey !== null,
      providerIdempotencyKey: providerIdempotencyKey
    };
  },
```

The projection has two opaque fields. `clientMutationId` is the client-minted
protocol identity; `settlementId` is the server-namespaced digest for the exact
mutation, authenticated principal, function, and arguments. Both are `null`
when the invocation carried no client mutation id. A settled duplicate returns
its stored result without handler re-entry. If an earlier attempt failed before
settlement and the handler genuinely re-enters, the same logical mutation sees
the same `settlementId` even though fresh per-entry values such as
`ctx.runtime.id()` may differ.

Treat both fields as opaque. Do not parse or re-hash a raw client mutation id,
and do not use a bearer token or secret as the provider key. Namespace the
server settlement id by effect, as the example does, so two providers do not
share one key.

Queries and actions have no mutation settlement identity and refuse the call
with `SNAPBACK_MUTATION_SETTLEMENT_UNAVAILABLE`. An action should call a named
mutation through `ctx.runMutation`; that mutation writes the effect intent and
the later action or worker performs delivery. The hosted coordinator currently
has no client-mutation replay ledger and returns the all-null twin, so a
replay-stable effect key is a local-target capability.

A mutation that declares a write to a `permissionBacking` table is generated
with `authorityCreating: true`. Authors may explicitly mark an opaque mutation
conservatively, but cannot clear a derived marker. Under the partial local
agent-auth slice this requires grant consent at admission, and the host still
enforces the exact permission-backing write dynamically.

## Read and delete through `ctx.db`

The mutation context exposes the same bounded query builder used by JS
queries. Start with `query(table)`, select a declared index with
`withIndex(indexName)`, and add one `eq(field, value)` per equality-bound index
field. `take(limit)` supplies the explicit row ceiling; `collect()` is the
terminal that executes the builder and returns the bounded array:

```js source=demos/messaging-snapback/snapback/functions.mjs fragment="bounded indexed collection inside startDirectMessage"
    const mine = await ctx.db
      .query('conversationMembers')
      .withIndex('by_user')
      .eq('userHandle', selfHandle)
      .take(500)
      .collect();
```

Do not omit the bound merely because the query uses an index: index selection
limits *which* rows qualify, while `take` limits how many qualifying rows the
handler can materialize. Chain compound-index equalities in declared index
field order.

These reads are caller-scoped by table visibility. A named mutation that has
already established authority with `ctx.permissions` may use the explicit
`ctx.db.elevated` read variants for protected facts needed by its invariant;
elevation never applies to `insert`, `patch`, or `delete`. Follow the
[authorization recipe](../auth/protecting-data.md#authorize-first-then-elevate-the-exact-handler-read),
including its cross-resource and non-member negative cases.

`delete(table, id)` buffers deletion of one row in the mutation's atomic write
set. A common toggle shape reads the indexed row first, then deletes by its
server-owned `_id`:

```js source=demos/messaging-snapback/snapback/functions.mjs fragment="indexed lookup and delete inside toggleReaction"
    const existing = await ctx.db
      .query('reactions')
      .withIndex('by_message_user_emoji')
      .eq('messageId', args.messageId)
      .eq('userHandle', args.userHandle)
      .eq('emoji', args.emoji)
      .first();
    if (existing) {
      await ctx.db.delete('reactions', existing._id);
      return { reacted: false };
    }
```

Here `first()` is the single-row terminal; use `take(...).collect()` when the
handler genuinely needs a bounded list. `delete` remains buffered until the
mutation commits, so a later refusal or conflict removes nothing.

## Consume the structured result

Successful direct mutations return one closed envelope:
`version`, `changed_count`, `result`, the server-derived
`authorityDescriptor` (persisted with the ACK proof; it grants no authority),
an optional deterministic `ctx_ledger`, nullable server-derived `attribution`
and `facts` (the active artifact generation), and the terminal `receipt`. The
todo acceptance proves the
created id, changed count, and server-owned row fields together:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const created = await db.mutate(api.createTodo, { args: { title: 'Buy milk' }, userId: ADA });
    assert(typeof created.result === 'string' && created.result.length > 0, 'no id returned');
    assertEqual(created.changed_count, 1, 'changed_count');
```

Use `results.value(validator)` for a direct scalar/object payload or
`results.document(table)` for one complete stored document. The generated
mutation reference carries that exact logical result type. Snapback validates
the post-JSON result against the frozen effective contract before committing
writes or retaining a successful settlement. A mismatch returns
`SNAPBACK_HANDLER_RESULT_CONTRACT_VIOLATION`; no write, durable version, or
successful settlement survives, and the diagnostic never echoes the rejected
value. The general result ceiling is 4 MiB, while retained mutation output
also keeps its existing 65,536-byte ceiling.

The violation details name the failing bound so you do not have to guess which
one it was: `constraint` carries one closed name (`maxResultBytes`, `maxBytes`,
`maxDepth`, `maxItems`, `minItems`, `nodeBudget`, `arity`, `dimensions`,
`requiredField`, `extraField`, `type`, `literal`, `range`, `union`, or
`serialize`) beside the JSON `path`, and size, count, depth, and budget bounds
also report numeric `limit` and `observed`. Those measurements are aggregate
magnitudes only — a rejected value, string, or dynamic key never appears.

An error is a structured `SNAPBACK_*` diagnostic. A rejected queued mutation
still has a terminal receipt on the error envelope so the client store can
settle it without guessing. A confirmed receipt always carries a non-null
durable `snapshotVersion`; `null` is allowed only for a rejected invocation
whose durable cursor could not be read safely.

## Refuse with a declared code, not a bare throw

<!-- since: 0.1.9 -->

**The rule: if a caller could act on the reason, declare it.** Write the
refusal code at the moment you write the guard — not after a test discovers
that the client cannot tell your business rule from a crash.

A bare `throw new Error('seat is taken')` reaches the caller as the platform
code `SNAPBACK_HANDLER_FAILED`, and the message text is deliberately *not* a
production or application contract. Direct native starts and production
launchers default to the redacted message `JavaScript handler failed` with
only the handler function in details; raw exception text remains on the
private error-tracking carrier. If the invocation-lifetime secret redactor
scrubs that private carrier, details may also contain the literal
`[REDACTED]` as a value-free witness that scrubbing occurred; no exception
text crosses the boundary. That is why refusal-first is a habit rather
than a polish step: the Zerobugs control shipped every
application-semantic refusal as a plain `throw` through ten receipted gate
attempts, and only adopted the channel when a gate assertion caught that a
short-id boundary refusal was invisible to the client
([issue](repo:issues/shelved/20260808-guide-gap-declared-refusals-discoverability.md)).

### Debug `SNAPBACK_HANDLER_FAILED` under the dev supervisor

The managed `snapback dev` and Vite development supervisors opt into a bounded
developer projection of the same failure. In that mode the diagnostic message
includes the validated JavaScript error class and underlying message. Its
details carry `errorClass` and `message`, plus `callee` and `property` when the
runtime can resolve the failed call, and `sourcePosition` with the handler
name, line, and column when the engine stack maps back into the handler source.
For example, `ctx.runtime.newId()` reports `property: "newId"` and
`callee: "ctx.runtime.newId"` instead of leaving only the generic code.

This visibility split is intentional: managed development favors the shortest
debugging loop, while production remains redacted by default because exception
messages and stacks can contain handler source, arguments, or other private
context. The enriched message is debugging evidence, not stable product copy;
declare a refusal code for any condition a client must branch on.

Declare a closed set of codes on the function:

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/refusal-tracking-authoring.test.mjs
  export const moveTodo = defineJsMutation({
    args: { id: v.id('todos') },
    writes: ['todos'],
    refusals: ['INVITE_CONSUMED', 'STALE_MOVE'],
    trackedRefusals: ['STALE_MOVE'],
    handler: async () => null,
  });
```

Then throw one of them with `ctx.refuse(code, details?)`. The declaration is
what types the throw — an undeclared code is *not* a smaller version of a
declared one, it is the generic failure:

```js source=tests/conformance/twin-corpus.handlers.js
  async declaredAppRefusal(ctx, args) {
    ctx.refuse('STALE_MOVE', { expected: 1, actual: args.revision });
  },
  async undeclaredAppRefusal(ctx) {
    ctx.refuse('SOMETHING_ELSE', { hidden: 'must-not-cross-admission' });
  },
```

Codes are uppercase `A-Z0-9_`, 1–64 characters, never the reserved
`SNAPBACK_` prefix, and at most 64 per function; codegen refuses a violation
with `FUNCTION_REFUSAL_DECLARATION_INVALID`. A declared refusal arrives as
the platform code `SNAPBACK_APP_REFUSAL` carrying `appCode` and `appDetails`
in `diagnostic.details`; it never masks a platform denial, and a refusing
mutation commits nothing. The host admits the claimed code only when the
invoked function declared it, and folds anything else — undeclared, forged,
or a bare `SNAPBACK_APP_REFUSAL` claim — to `SNAPBACK_HANDLER_FAILED` with
the app payload dropped. `ctx.refuse` returns `never`, so it needs no
`throw` at the call site, and queries and actions have exactly the same
channel.

### Decide what deserves a code

Ask what the caller would do with the answer:

| Reason | Channel |
| --- | --- |
| The caller can retry differently, pick another value, or be shown copy ("seat taken", "invite already used", "stale revision") | **Declare it.** `refusals: [...]` + `ctx.refuse` |
| The caller must reconcile a concurrent write | Already typed: `SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT` |
| The caller is not allowed to do this | Already typed: the auth codes, e.g. `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PERMISSION_DENIED` |
| A bug, an impossible state, or an invariant the caller cannot influence | Leave it a bare `throw`; the generic fold is correct |

Refusal codes are your product's vocabulary, so keep them stable: they end up
in UI copy switches and in tests. To make one issue-eligible in
[error tracking](../operating/error-tracking.md), also list it in
`trackedRefusals` (a narrowing of `refusals`, never an admission by itself).

The consuming side — matching `appCode` through optimistic rollback rather
than parsing message text — is
[show stable application errors](../clients/react.md#show-stable-application-errors-through-rollback).

**Declarative host-plan mutations are a different channel.** `elseError` on
`get(...)` and the code on `guard(...)` are plan refusals: that code arrives
as `diagnostic.code` itself, not wrapped in `SNAPBACK_APP_REFUSAL` with an
`appCode`. Every application plan code must also be declared in `refusals`;
codegen and server artifact validation reject omissions, while reserved
`SNAPBACK_` platform codes are exempt. That declaration cross-check does not
unify the runtime envelopes. Match plan refusals on `diagnostic.code` and
JS-handler refusals on `details.appCode`; do not write one client branch
expecting both shapes. The plan channel's complete semantics are
[refusals from a plan](./declarative-plans.md#refuse-from-a-plan-elseerror-and-guard).

## Preserve invariants with read sets

JS mutation reads are captured by the server. Declarative host-plan mutations
that depend on an earlier client observation carry that explicit
`readSet`. At commit, Snapback validates the exact row or predicate
dependencies. If a concurrent writer changed a dependency, the whole mutation
is rejected as `SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT`:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const err = await assertThrows(
      () => db.mutate(api.setCompleted, {
        args: { id, completed: false },
        userId: ADA,
        readSet: [{ table: 'todos', id, version: observed }],
      }),
      'SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT',
      'expected conflict',
    );
```

Treat that diagnostic as an invariant failure to reconcile, not as permission
to force a last-writer-wins commit. Predicate-shaped captured reads are
validated at predicate granularity, so unrelated writes do not spuriously
conflict.

Authorization-protected writes have one additional pre-transaction conflict:
`SNAPBACK_AUTH_RESERVATION_STALE`. It is HTTP 409 with
`details.retryable: true`, `details.effectCommitted: false`, and
`details.retryStrategy: "short-jitter"`. The standard JavaScript and Swift
clients recognize only that exact closed refusal and retry the complete write
within a bounded short-jitter budget. They do not retry a missing fact, a
different status, an ambiguous outcome, or anything that may have committed.
Every retry remains pinned to the first attempt's exact authority/carrier
generation; logout, user switch, or credential replacement fails the operation
stale instead of replaying predecessor intent as the successor.
Do not add an application retry loop, treat it as backend downtime, or use
service-style exponential backoff.

The JavaScript client defaults to 40 total attempts with 20–80 ms jitter.
Configure `reservationRetryMaxAttempts` (use `1` to disable retries) and
`reservationRetryJitterMilliseconds: [minimum, maximum]` at construction.
Inspect `reservationRetryDiagnostics()` or provide
`onReservationRetryDiagnostic` to retain scheduled, settled, and exhausted
attempt evidence without changing mutation settlement.

Tests for an authorization rule must assert the intended denial code
(`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PERMISSION_DENIED`, for example), not merely that the write
failed. A stale reservation is contention, not evidence that the rule ran.

## Declare structural uniqueness

For one-row-per-key application invariants, declare a true unique index instead
of scanning in the handler:

```js source=demos/shindig/snapback/schema.mjs
    .index('by_user', ['userId'])
    .index('by_event', ['eventId'])
    .index('by_event_user', ['eventId', 'userId'], { unique: true })
    .sync(),
```

Unique indexes may be compound. Every key field must be required in v1 so the
constraint is total across SQLite and Postgres. Duplicate inserts that reach
the serialized write boundary race at the constraint: exactly one wins, every
loser commits nothing and receives `SNAPBACK_UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION`. A
larger mutation may still fail earlier at an authorization or stale-reservation
boundary, also without committing. Snapback does not currently ship `upsert`;
keep duplicate-as-error flows as inserts and handle the unique diagnostic.

## Bound and resume bulk work

One mutation may buffer at most **1,024 writes**. The ceiling includes ordinary
`ctx.db` writes and other writes expanded into the same commit, such as
membership commands and maintained-projection effects. Attempting a 1,025th
write rejects the whole mutation with
`SNAPBACK_BUFFERED_WRITE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`; none of its buffered writes commit.

Snapback does not ship a separate bulk-mutation or resumable-mutation API.
Build large jobs from the ordinary bounded primitives:

1. Read a bounded page through a stable unique index and keyset cursor; see
   [safe standard patterns](./standard-patterns.md#generate-keyset-pages).
2. Send that page to one ordinary mutation, sized so its direct writes plus
   generated projection effects remain at or below 1,024.
3. In that same mutation, update an application-owned job row with the last
   completed cursor or stable key.
4. Read that checkpoint before the next page. After interruption, resume after
   the committed checkpoint rather than replaying every earlier page.

For the specific case of loading a deterministic acceptance fixture larger
than one seed or one mutation allows, the paved recipe — gated batch-ingest
mutation, loader session, digest verification — is
[loading large deterministic fixtures](../testing/large-fixtures.md).

Each page is its own atomic commit; the whole multi-page job is not one
transaction. Make each page idempotent under the application's business key or
current status, and advance the checkpoint only in the commit that applied the
page. Keep batches comfortably below the ceiling when one input can expand into
multiple projection or membership writes. If the product invariant requires
more than 1,024 changes to commit all-or-nothing, redesign that invariant rather
than disguising several mutations as one transaction.

## One commit, one version

All affected rows share the mutation's `version`; no-op writes do not advance
it. Durable live delivery is produced from the committed write set, so clients
never observe a partial mutation. The version is a logical ordering within one
app database, not a wall-clock timestamp. It is an exact integer in
`0..=Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. The maximum commit is usable, but an operation
that needs its successor fails before writing with
`SNAPBACK_STORAGE_VERSION_EXHAUSTED`; never round or synthesize a cursor.

## Retain bounded record history

By default a committed write replaces the prior row image. A table that needs
its recent prior versions retained inside storage — the substrate host
machinery uses to prove facts about past states — declares finite per-record
history on the schema:

```ts source=packages/snapback-codegen/history-authoring-types.fixture.ts
const policy: HistoryRetentionSpec = {
  retainMs: 60_000,
  maxVersionsPerRecord: 12,
};

defineTable({ title: v.string() }).history(policy).sync();
```

The declaration is a closed typed object of exactly `retainMs` (an integer
from 1 through 2,592,000,000 — at most 30 days) and `maxVersionsPerRecord`
(1 through 1,000), declared at most once per table; there is deliberately no
unbounded spelling. It activates atomically with schema publication: central
writers then capture each committed change into the bounded history store,
and pruning enforces both the age window and the per-record version cap.

Retained versions are storage-side facts consumed by host machinery — the
operation ledger's historical-owner reads when it explains an owner
mutation, and the instance-fork promotion proof tail — not an application
read surface. There is no author-facing history query: a JS handler cannot
read a row's prior versions, and an app that needs user-visible revision
history keeps modeling it as ordinary application rows. Declaring
`history()` without a reason costs a write and storage per commit for
nothing.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not implement read-then-write invariants as two unrelated requests.**
  Read inside the JS mutation or carry the explicit host-plan baseline.
- **Do not scan to emulate a unique compound key.** Declare a unique index;
  read sets are conflict detection, not a substitute for structural uniqueness.
- **Do not swallow `SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT`.** Reconcile or ask the user;
  blind retry may violate the invariant that caused the read.
- **Do not signal an application-semantic refusal with a bare `throw`.** The
  message is not a public contract and the caller receives only
  `SNAPBACK_HANDLER_FAILED`; declare the code in `refusals` and raise it with
  `ctx.refuse`.
- **Do not invent an ad-hoc `{ ok: false, error }` result shape** to carry a
  domain error past the result contract. A refusal is a rejection: it commits
  nothing and settles the client's optimistic layer correctly, which a
  successful-looking envelope does not.
- **Do not count `SNAPBACK_AUTH_RESERVATION_STALE` as an authorization-rule
  denial.** Let the standard client retry the exact effect-free refusal, then
  assert the rule's exact code.
- **Do not set `_id`, `_version`, `_createdAt`, or `_updatedAt`.**
  They are server-owned.
- **Do not send an unbounded collection to one mutation.** Page by a stable
  key, commit a bounded batch with its application checkpoint, and resume from
  the last committed checkpoint.
- **Do not infer success from HTTP status alone.** Consume the result,
  diagnostic, and terminal receipt envelope.
- **Do not omit a result contract when callers depend on the payload shape.**
  Omission deliberately generates `unknown`.
- **Do not validate a mutation result after committing.** The runtime-owned
  pre-commit validator is what makes result-contract failure atomic.

{
  "seedVersion": "clique.explicit.v1",
  "tables": {
    "users": [],
    "follows": [],

import {
  AUTH_DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_GUEST_RETENTION_MS,
  defineAuth,
  defineEphemeral,
  defineSchema,
  defineTable,
  v,
} from '@expo/snapback-codegen/define';
import { typing } from './surface-model.mjs';

const authProgram = defineAuth({
  version: 1,
  custody: 'durable-required',
  mechanisms: {
    guest: { kind: 'guest' },
    password: {
      kind: 'password',
      identifier: 'email',
      provider: 'builtIn',
      recovery: 'recoveryCodes',
    },
  },
  assuranceRequirements: {},
  recoveryPolicy: {
    recoveryCodes: {
      enabled: true,
      requiredWhen: 'no-independent-recovery',
      rotateAfterUse: true,
      plaintextCustody: 'one-time-response',
    },
    lastAuthenticator: 'enforce',
  },
  guestPolicy: {
    enabled: true,
    claiming: [],
    reaping: {
      afterMs: AUTH_DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_GUEST_RETENTION_MS,
      cleanup: { kind: 'declarative', default: 'tombstone', tables: {} },
    },
  },
  secretReferences: {},
});

const postKind = v.union([
  v.literal('text'),
  v.literal('images'),
  v.literal('video'),
]);
const conversationKind = v.union([v.literal('dm'), v.literal('group')]);
const membershipRole = v.union([v.literal('member'), v.literal('admin')]);

export default defineSchema(
  {
    users: defineTable({
      principal: v.principal(),
      email: v.string(),
      handle: v.string(),
      displayName: v.string(),
      bio: v.string(),
      location: v.string(),
      link: v.string(),
      avatarUri: v.string(),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
      updatedAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_principal', ['principal'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_email', ['email'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_handle', ['handle'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_display_name', ['displayName'])
      .sync(),

    follows: defineTable({
      followerId: v.id('users'),
      followingId: v.id('users'),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_pair', ['followerId', 'followingId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_follower', ['followerId'])
      .index('by_following', ['followingId'])
      .sync(),

    posts: defineTable({
      externalId: v.string(),
      authorId: v.id('users'),
      kind: postKind,
      text: v.string(),
      imageUris: v.array(v.string()),
      videoUri: v.string(),
      parentId: v.optional(v.id('posts')),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
      updatedAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_external_id', ['externalId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_created', ['createdAt'])
      .index('by_author_created', ['authorId', 'createdAt'])
      .index('by_parent_created', ['parentId', 'createdAt'])
      .sync(),

    likes: defineTable({
      postId: v.id('posts'),
      userId: v.id('users'),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_post_user', ['postId', 'userId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_post', ['postId'])
      .index('by_user', ['userId'])
      .sync(),

    reposts: defineTable({
      postId: v.id('posts'),
      userId: v.id('users'),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_post_user', ['postId', 'userId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_post', ['postId'])
      .index('by_user_created', ['userId', 'createdAt'])
      .index('by_created', ['createdAt'])
      .sync(),

    conversations: defineTable({
      externalId: v.string(),
      kind: conversationKind,
      pairKey: v.optional(v.string()),
      name: v.string(),
      description: v.string(),
      creatorId: v.id('users'),
      lastPreview: v.string(),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
      updatedAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_external_id', ['externalId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_pair_key', ['pairKey'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_updated', ['updatedAt'])
      .sync(),

    memberships: defineTable({
      conversationId: v.id('conversations'),
      userId: v.id('users'),
      role: membershipRole,
      active: v.boolean(),
      joinedAt: v.integer(),
      leftAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_conversation_user', ['conversationId', 'userId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_user', ['userId'])
      .index('by_conversation', ['conversationId'])
      .sync(),

    messages: defineTable({
      externalId: v.string(),
      conversationId: v.id('conversations'),
      senderId: v.id('users'),
      text: v.string(),
      quoteMessageId: v.optional(v.id('messages')),
      createdAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_external_id', ['externalId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_conversation_created', ['conversationId', 'createdAt'])
      .sync(),

    receipts: defineTable({
      conversationId: v.id('conversations'),
      messageId: v.id('messages'),
      userId: v.id('users'),
      state: v.integer(),
      required: v.boolean(),
      updatedAt: v.integer(),
    })
      .visibility({ kind: 'public-read' })
      .index('by_message_user', ['messageId', 'userId'], { unique: true })
      .index('by_message', ['messageId'])
      .index('by_user_conversation', ['userId', 'conversationId'])
      .sync(),
  },
  {
    auth: { mode: 'sessions' },
    authProgram,
    ephemeral: defineEphemeral({ typing }),
  },
);

Password login is a credential class on the ordinary [sessions surface](./sessions-and-principals.md). A successful signin runs the same session-creation core as an email-code exchange and returns the same credential response. There is **no parallel identity system, no parallel token, and no separate session shape** — one principal, several credentials. This is the first sign-in method a browser app can offer end users without a mail adapter. These verbs need no admin token and no impersonation capability. They are the product front door, not an operator impersonation path — unlike `snapback session mint`. ## What a failed signin tells an attacker: nothing Wrong password, unknown identifier, and locked-out all answer the **same** `SNAPBACK_AUTH_CREDENTIAL_INVALID` with the same status, body, headers, and timing envelope. It never contains the password hash. The corresponding AdminWrite `snapback auth password unlock` verb deletes that ledger row early. Real reset waits on the LLP 0045 mail adapter. Recovery codes are the self-serve path in the meantime. - **Reset is same-principal only.** The address's `email-code` identity and its password identity must belong to the same principal. A password-only account, an email-code-only account, and the two-principal squat state all refuse uniformly — transferring a squatter's credential to someone who later proves the address is exactly the hijack this contains. - **A password never proves you own the email address.** It proves control of the account whose login name is that string. Only an email-code exchange proves address ownership, and the two claims are separate identity rows in separate provider namespaces. A password identity can never satisfy an email-code lookup. - **Catalog v4 is required.** A store created by an older runtime keeps working for everything else and reports the password provider unready — it does not fail. There is no silent migration. - **Sender-constrained custody is refused, not downgraded.** When sender-constrained credentials are active, password methods refuse with a typed error rather than quietly falling back to bearer-only custody. ## Anti-patterns - **Do not construct `AuthCoordinator` or call an authority-adoption method in an ordinary React/Expo app.** The generated application client and provider own that composition; the explicit seam is for custom brokers and shells. - **Do not discard, log, analyze, or silently persist signup recovery codes.** Present the one-time projection immediately and hand custody to the user. - **Do not implement user switch as sign-in over an authenticated principal.** Sign out, wait for settled anonymous, then enter the successor account. - **Do not infer Expo-native restoration from browser or Expo-web evidence.** The iOS and Android `single-runtime` arms have separate Phase-2 receipts and ship in the published 0.1.24 closure (first publish recorded in the [closed custody first-publish gate](repo:issues/closed/20260816-custody-first-publish-gate.md)). The iOS extension evidence is share-sheet-kind-only; NSE/`simctl push` remains a nonclaim. - **Do not generalize this local bearer journey into hosted or sender-constrained auth.** Check [Targets](./targets.md) first.

Everything else stays byte-shape-identical to `/auth/exchange`. ## Recovery codes are the recovery path Signup returns eight one-time recovery codes. **They are shown exactly once** and are not readable again — not through the admin console, not through any route. There is **no parallel identity system, no parallel token, and no separate session shape** — one principal, several credentials. An app with no declared password mechanism keeps the existing username-v1 default. The choice is stored in catalog v4 at the first sessions activation and is immutable afterward; codegen/startup refuses a later contradictory declaration with `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_IDENTIFIER_MODE_IMMUTABLE` instead of reinterpreting existing identities. The default password minimum is 12 decoded UTF-8 bytes. To choose a different app-wide minimum, set `minimumLength` on the password mechanism: ```js fragment reason="policy-only excerpt from the defineAuth password mechanism shown above" password: { kind: 'password', identifier: 'email', provider: 'builtIn', recovery: 'recoveryCodes', minimumLength: 8, } ``` The declaration is a safe integer from 8 through 128; every password mechanism in one program must resolve to the same value or codegen refuses `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_CONFLICT`. A cold password-only app still settles a server-witnessed anonymous principal so the entry form is reachable; generated `anonymousPublic` controls anonymous app-data access, not whether boot can finish. Only the `authenticated` arm has a current `userId`. The template's account UI also makes the recovery handoff explicit: ```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/src/App.tsx {recoveryCodes ? (

{recoveryCodes.join('\n')}
) : null} ``` The application must hand those codes to the user for separate safe custody at signup. On a full browser reload, construct the same app client again. Browser and Expo web use IndexedDB plus Web Locks, so the owner restores the settled principal without another signup or sign-in. `dispose()` only releases the process projection; it does not sign out or delete durable custody. 4. After either, the client holds an ordinary session: protected queries, refresh, the logout barrier, and reload restoration all behave exactly as they do after an email-code exchange. Both methods require an `AuthCoordinator` and an anonymous predecessor — they create a fresh authority, so they adopt through the same anonymous-issuance path `authExchange` uses. The bearer is never returned to your code; the coordinator owns it. An ordinary React or Expo app should not construct that coordinator itself; use the application-client/provider journey above. ## The exact session shape Two different shapes carry the user id, at two layers. Signup additionally returns `recoveryCodes` — the only response that carries a sixth field. Everything else stays byte-shape-identical to `/auth/exchange`. ## Recovery codes are the recovery path Signup returns eight one-time recovery codes. **They are shown exactly once** and are not readable again — not through the admin console, not through any route. Store them at signup or lose them. - `authRecoveryConsume({ email, code })` mints a session and automatically replaces the whole set. A consumed code cannot be reused. - `authRecoveryRotate()` replaces the set for an authenticated principal — use it after suspected disclosure. Change is a **same-authority rotation**, not a new login: it rotates the acting session's bearer, keeps the authority instance id, and revokes the user's *other* sessions. A session belonging to a different user is untouched. Because the authority is preserved, the client adopts it through the same rotation path refresh uses. `authPasswordSet({ newPassword, stepUp })` adds a first password to a principal that has none. They are the product front door, not an operator impersonation path — unlike `snapback session mint`. ## What a failed signin tells an attacker: nothing Wrong password, unknown identifier, and locked-out all answer the **same** `SNAPBACK_AUTH_CREDENTIAL_INVALID` with the same status, body, headers, and timing envelope. A signin against an address with no account still performs a full key-derivation against a dummy hash so the cost is uniform. Lock state is deliberately **invisible on the wire**. Lock existence, threshold, and expiry are observable only through the authenticated admin projection and `authProgramReadiness`. An operator can call `admin.passwordAttempt(email)`. Its AdminRead response contains the declared `failureThreshold`, `failureWindowMs`, and `lockDurationMs`, plus either `attempt: null` or the canonical identifier, window start, failed count, lock deadline, and current `locked` bit. harness itself makes green structurally impossible, record the exact instrument
failure rather than relabeling it.

Create run-log.md immediately. Its first lines must record lane id sol-clique-explicit,
model gpt-5.6-sol, effort=xhigh, backend=snapback-explicit-0.1.25, and
start=<epoch>. Append timestamped lines at every milestone start, green or
failure, error, retry, workaround, correction loop (each with an attribution:
snapback-defect, agent-error, environment, or ambiguous, plus an evidence
pointer), and knowledge lookup. Record every server PID you start and kill only
those PIDs at the end; never use pkill/killall/pattern kills. Use only ports
42000–42019 for every server you start and pass the app origin
to choreography through `CHOREO_BASE_URL`. The safety limit is four hours per
milestone; on exhaustion record capability-failure and obey dependency
blocking.

At each milestone boundary append to diary.md: what you built, what felt easy,
what fought you, what the explicit profile saved or cost, and what
documentation or diagnostic was missing. After M3, before tallying any numbers,
write a 1–2 page qualitative essay.md comparing this experience to backends you
know (Convex, Supabase, Firebase, hand-rolled Postgres+Express). Then write
final-report.md with raw start/end epochs and wall by milestone, first-green
times, correction loops and attribution, suite/choreography results,
package/runtime pins, source-inspection events, and a candid gap list. End with
end=<epoch>.

## Observation-controller handoff (instrument 0.3.3-m8)

The external lane controller owns the authoring clock and is already running.
For each milestone, run the suite and choreography with their required typed
observation outputs, then make this your final command for that milestone:

  node "/Users/ccheever/bench-matrix-20260823-r2/runner/benchmarks/tools/social-messenger/metering/r2-cell-signal.mjs" --root "/Users/ccheever/bench-matrix-20260823-r2/cells/sol-clique-explicit" --milestone M1 \
    --status green --terminal-reason green \
    --suite-status suite-status.json \
    --suite-observations receipts/m1-suite.observations.jsonl \
    --choreography-receipt receipts/m1-choreography.jsonl \
    --choreography-observations receipts/m1-choreography.jsonl.observations.jsonl

Replace M1/m1 for M2 and M3. The signal validates paths and blocks until the
controller opens the next milestone, preserving one continuous native harness
session while preventing observation windows from overlapping. For a terminal
failure, use status aborted/terminal-reason abort, or capability-failure with
terminal-reason wall-cap or token-cap, and retain every sidecar that exists.
Never hand-author aggregate metering or record fields; the controller derives
them from the native stream, typed observations, receipts, and these terminal
signals. Finish diary.md, essay.md, and final-report.md before sending M3;
the M3 signal is the last authoring action before the native harness exits.

## Skills
A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and source locator. `file` locators are on the host filesystem, `executor package` locators are owned by their execution environment, `orchestrator package` locators are opaque package identifiers, and `custom resource` locators use their provider's access mechanism.
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/skills/.system/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/skills/.system/openai-docs/SKILL.md)

Use when Codex needs to create a new personal plugin, add optional plugin structure, generate or update marketplace entries for plugin ordering and availability metadata, or update an existing local plugin during development with the CLI-driven cachebuster and reinstall flow. (file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/skills/.system/plugin-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- browser:control-in-app-browser: Control the in-app Browser for opening, navigating, inspecting visible or interactive page state, clicking, typing, screenshots, and local web testing. It can have existing signed-in sessions. For semantic operations on linked resources, prefer a purpose-built connector, API, or CLI when available. (file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled/browser/26.810.50856/skills/control-in-app-browser/SKILL.md)

(file: /Users/ccheever/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-primary-runtime/documents/26.819.11345/skills/documents/SKILL.md)

R2_CELL_SIGNAL_INVALID: --help requires a value
# Social-messenger choreography harness

This directory contains the P2-hardened Playwright harness for Clique's
milestone choreography, extended for M8. It launches isolated Alice and Bob
browser contexts, adds Carol for M5 and a second same-account Alice context for
M8, signs them in through the contract's `sm-auth-*` IDs, runs selected `m1()`
through `m6()` and `m8()` segments, and writes structured JSONL receipts.

The harness consumes only test IDs frozen in `../CONTRACT.md`. A runtime guard
rejects any other ID. It never turns missing automation surface into a pass.

## Setup and usage

The instrument intentionally has no lockfile before P3 freeze. A runner must
provision the pinned Playwright and AJV dependencies from `package.json` and the
selected Playwright browser.

```sh
cd benchmarks/tools/social-messenger/choreography
npm install
npx playwright install chromium

CHOREO_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:5173 \
CHOREO_PASSWORD='fixture-password' \
volta run --node 24.18.0 node choreography.mjs m3 \
  --suite-status /absolute/path/suite-status.json
```

`npm test` starts a tiny calibration app, executes M1 and M8 through the real
multi-context harness, validates every emitted receipt against
`receipts.schema.json`, and requires honest segment greens. The app implements
the M8 likes, multi-device unread, live-message, and warm-offline queue surfaces
instead of short-circuiting browser observations. A second M8 run deliberately
serves stale Insights and must exit non-green. The test also exercises the pure
aggregation edge cases: optional skip, required skip, and implemented failure.

The positional segment argument is optional and defaults to `all`. It accepts
`all`, one milestone (`m1` ... `m6` or `m8`), or a comma-separated ordered
subset such as `m1,m3,m8`. `all` runs M1–M6 followed by M8; M7 remains the
brief's separate fresh-session milestone and has no web choreography segment.

Scoring DAG: M3 requires M1 only; M3 does not require M2. Reduced-run
protocol: execute M1, then M2, then M3 in that order. Do not start M3 to
avoid an unfinished M2. A reduced run that skips M2 is non-conforming even
though M3's scoring prerequisite is only M1.

Every implemented CLI flag is:

- `--browser <chromium|firefox|webkit>` — browser engine; default `chromium`.
- `--headed` — show both browser windows; default is headless.
- `--receipts <path>` — JSONL destination; default is `receipts.jsonl` beside
  `choreography.mjs`. The file is truncated at the beginning of each run.
- `--observations <path>` — typed D0.6 assertion-attempt/wait stream; defaults
  to `<receipts>.observations.jsonl`. The metering manifest hash-binds this
  stream before it projects the choreography-owned browser-wait counts. Each
  attempt records only actual locator, predicate, or page-event settlement
  intervals; setup/action and other attempt wall are excluded.
- `--lane-run-id <id>` — required stable lane identity, shared with the
  metering manifest (`CHOREO_LANE_RUN_ID` is the environment form).
- `--suite-status <path>` — required JSON object keyed by milestone. Every
  selected segment must have `{ "pass": boolean, "receipt": string|null }`.
  The runner validates this complete linkage before credentials, Playwright,
  receipt creation, or browser startup. A passing value must carry a non-empty
  suite evidence pointer in `receipt`. Receipt paths are relative to the
  suite-status file, must remain under its directory, and are statted and
  SHA-256 digested before startup. The digest is retained in the segment
  summary so the meter can detect a change when it writes the record.
- `--adapter <path>` — optional lane navigation/fixture adapter. It carries
  route paths and fixture choices only; it cannot report outcomes or bypass
  browser observations. The built-in adapter uses `/profile/{handle}`,
  `/profile/edit`, `/settings`, `/search`, and `/insights` plus the committed
  fixture pack. `routes.insights` may override the M8 Insights route.
- `--simulator-status <path>` — optional separately recorded M6/M8 simulator
  statuses. A single legacy status object is accepted, as is a bundle keyed by
  `m6` and/or `m8`; entries use `{ "id":"ios-simulator-m6"|
  "ios-simulator-m8", "pass":true|false|null, "receipt":string|null,
  "reason":string|null }`. Each entry is retained only in its matching summary
  and never gates web green; see `simulator.md`.
- `--timeout <ms>` — positive integer timeout for ordinary UI observations;
  default `10000`. The M3 2-second appearance and 5-second expiry ceilings are
  fixed by the brief and are not relaxed by this flag.
- `--help` — print usage without loading Playwright.

Exit code `0` means every selected segment has `green:true` (suite plus complete
required choreography). Exit code `1` means execution completed but at least one
segment was not green because a required check was skipped, an implemented
check failed, or suite evidence was absent/failing. Exit code `2` is
configuration or fatal harness failure.

## Environment variables

- `CHOREO_BASE_URL` — required lane web URL.
- `CHOREO_LANE_RUN_ID` — required stable lane identity unless
  `--lane-run-id` is supplied.
- `CHOREO_PASSWORD` — shared fixture password fallback for Alice, Bob, and Carol;
  Alice's M8 second context uses the same Alice credential.
- `CHOREO_ALICE_PASSWORD`, `CHOREO_BOB_PASSWORD` — per-persona passwords;
  `CHOREO_CAROL_PASSWORD` is also required for M5 unless the shared fallback is
  set. Passwords have no CLI flags so
  they do not appear in the process command line.
- `CHOREO_ALICE_EMAIL`, `CHOREO_BOB_EMAIL`, `CHOREO_CAROL_EMAIL` — optional;
  defaults are the corresponding `@example.com` personas from `CONTRACT.md`.
- `CHOREO_BROWSER` — default for `--browser`.
- `CHOREO_RECEIPTS` — default for `--receipts`.
- `CHOREO_OBSERVATIONS` — default for the typed assertion-wait sidecar.
- `CHOREO_SUITE_STATUS` — default for `--suite-status`.
- `CHOREO_ADAPTER` — default for `--adapter`.

This directory contains the P2-hardened Playwright harness for Clique's
milestone choreography, extended for M8. It launches isolated Alice and Bob
browser contexts, adds Carol for M5 and a second same-account Alice context for
M8, signs them in through the contract's `sm-auth-*` IDs, runs selected `m1()`
through `m6()` and `m8()` segments, and writes structured JSONL receipts.

The harness consumes only test IDs frozen in `../CONTRACT.md`. A runtime guard
rejects any other ID. It never turns missing automation surface into a pass.

## Setup and usage

The instrument intentionally has no lockfile before P3 freeze. A runner must
provision the pinned Playwright and AJV dependencies from `package.json` and the
selected Playwright browser.

```sh
cd benchmarks/tools/social-messenger/choreography
npm install
npx playwright install chromium

CHOREO_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:5173 \
CHOREO_PASSWORD='fixture-password' \
volta run --node 24.18.0 node choreography.mjs m3 \
  --suite-status /absolute/path/suite-status.json
```

`npm test` starts a tiny calibration app, executes M1 and M8 through the real
multi-context harness, validates every emitted receipt against
`receipts.schema.json`, and requires honest segment greens. The app implements
the M8 likes, multi-device unread, live-message, and warm-offline queue surfaces
instead of short-circuiting browser observations. A second M8 run deliberately
serves stale Insights and must exit non-green. The test also exercises the pure
aggregation edge cases: optional skip, required skip, and implemented failure.

The positional segment argument is optional and defaults to `all`. It accepts

subset such as `m1,m3,m8`. `all` runs M1–M6 followed by M8; M7 remains the
brief's separate fresh-session milestone and has no web choreography segment.

protocol: execute M1, then M2, then M3 in that order. Do not start M3 to
avoid an unfinished M2. A reduced run that skips M2 is non-conforming even
though M3's scoring prerequisite is only M1.

Every implemented CLI flag is:

- `--browser <chromium|firefox|webkit>` — browser engine; default `chromium`.
- `--headed` — show both browser windows; default is headless.
- `--receipts <path>` — JSONL destination; default is `receipts.jsonl` beside
  `choreography.mjs`. The file is truncated at the beginning of each run.

  to `<receipts>.observations.jsonl`. The metering manifest hash-binds this
  stream before it projects the choreography-owned browser-wait counts. Each
  attempt records only actual locator, predicate, or page-event settlement
  intervals; setup/action and other attempt wall are excluded.
- `--lane-run-id <id>` — required stable lane identity, shared with the
  metering manifest (`CHOREO_LANE_RUN_ID` is the environment form).
- `--suite-status <path>` — required JSON object keyed by milestone. Every
  selected segment must have `{ "pass": boolean, "receipt": string|null }`.

  receipt creation, or browser startup. A passing value must carry a non-empty
  suite evidence pointer in `receipt`. Receipt paths are relative to the
  suite-status file, must remain under its directory, and are statted and
  SHA-256 digested before startup. The digest is retained in the segment
  summary so the meter can detect a change when it writes the record.
- `--adapter <path>` — optional lane navigation/fixture adapter. It carries
  route paths and fixture choices only; it cannot report outcomes or bypass
  browser observations. The built-in adapter uses `/profile/{handle}`,
  `/profile/edit`, `/settings`, `/search`, and `/insights` plus the committed
  fixture pack. `routes.insights` may override the M8 Insights route.
- `--simulator-status <path>` — optional separately recorded M6/M8 simulator

  `m6` and/or `m8`; entries use `{ "id":"ios-simulator-m6"|

  and never gates web green; see `simulator.md`.
- `--timeout <ms>` — positive integer timeout for ordinary UI observations;
  default `10000`. The M3 2-second appearance and 5-second expiry ceilings are
  fixed by the brief and are not relaxed by this flag.
- `--help` — print usage without loading Playwright.

required choreography). Exit code `1` means execution completed but at least one
segment was not green because a required check was skipped, an implemented
check failed, or suite evidence was absent/failing. Exit code `2` is
configuration or fatal harness failure.

# Social-messenger choreography harness

This directory contains the P2-hardened Playwright harness for Clique's
milestone choreography, extended for M8. It launches isolated Alice and Bob
browser contexts, adds Carol for M5 and a second same-account Alice context for
M8, signs them in through the contract's `sm-auth-*` IDs, runs selected `m1()`
through `m6()` and `m8()` segments, and writes structured JSONL receipts.

The harness consumes only test IDs frozen in `../CONTRACT.md`. A runtime guard
rejects any other ID. It never turns missing automation surface into a pass.

## Setup and usage

The instrument intentionally has no lockfile before P3 freeze. A runner must
provision the pinned Playwright and AJV dependencies from `package.json` and the
selected Playwright browser.

```sh
cd benchmarks/tools/social-messenger/choreography
npm install
npx playwright install chromium

CHOREO_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:5173 \
CHOREO_PASSWORD='fixture-password' \
volta run --node 24.18.0 node choreography.mjs m3 \
  --suite-status /absolute/path/suite-status.json
```

`npm test` starts a tiny calibration app, executes M1 and M8 through the real
multi-context harness, validates every emitted receipt against
`receipts.schema.json`, and requires honest segment greens. The app implements

serves stale Insights and must exit non-green. The test also exercises the pure

---
name: control-in-app-browser
description: "Control the in-app Browser for opening, navigating, inspecting visible or interactive page state, clicking, typing, screenshots, and local web testing. It can have existing signed-in sessions. For semantic operations on linked resources, prefer a purpose-built connector, API, or CLI when available."
---

# Browser
## Stop: choose the right surface before any browser action
Explicit browser intent wins: if the user names the in-app browser or Chrome, or asks to open, show, or navigate to a page; inspect its visual or interactive state; or interact with its UI, continue with Browser and do not substitute a connector.

Otherwise, treat a URL or open browser tab as context, not browser intent. Earlier Browser use does not make later semantic work browser-first. Before each semantic operation on a linked resource, you MUST query available and deferred tools for an applicable connector, API, or CLI. Reading this skill or scanning visible tools does not count. Do not initialize Browser for that operation until the query is complete. Use the non-browser tool when available. If it handles the current operation, continue the larger workflow without Browser for that operation. Use Browser when no such tool exists, the tool cannot access the resource or lacks a required capability, or UI work remains; use available browser context before asking the user to repeat it.

Use this skill for browser automation tasks such as inspecting pages, navigating, testing local apps, clicking, typing, taking screenshots, and reading visible page state.

If this plugin is listed as available in the session, treat that as mandatory reading before browser work. Open and follow this skill before saying that Browser is unavailable and before falling back to standalone Playwright or Computer Use.

Do not skip this skill just because Computer Use MCP tool calls are directly visible or appear easier to invoke. The presence of Computer Use tools is not evidence that Computer Use is the preferred browser surface.

## Setup Documentation
Use `await agent.documentation.get("<name>")` when one of these setup topics applies:
- `bootstrap-troubleshooting`: read when browser setup succeeds but discovery or selection fails
- `chrome-troubleshooting`: read when Chromium browser extension setup, installation, or communication fails

## Bootstrap
These setup details are internal. User-facing progress updates should be less technical in nature. Never mention `Node REPL`, `node_repl`, `REPL`, JavaScript sessions, module exports, reading documentation, or loading instructions unless a user is asking for that exact information. If setup or recovery is needed, describe it naturally as connecting to the browser or retrying the browser connection.

The `browser-client` module is the core entry point for browser use, and is available under `scripts/browser-client.mjs` in this plugin's root directory. ALWAYS import it using an absolute path. IMPORTANT: If this path cannot be found, stop and report that this plugin is missing `scripts/browser-client.mjs`. NEVER use the built in `browser-client` library.

Run browser setup code through the Node REPL `js` tool. In this environment the callable tool id typically appears as `mcp__node_repl__js`. If it is not already available, use tool discovery for `node_repl js` without setting a result limit. You need the `js` execution tool: `js_reset` only clears state, and `js_add_node_module_dir` only changes package resolution. Do not call either helper while trying to expose `js`. If `js` is still not available, search again for `node_repl js` with `limit: 10`.

CODE MODE REQUIREMENT: When you call the Node REPL `js` tool from the code-mode `exec` tool, the outer `exec` script containing the initial `documentation()` call MUST begin with `// @exec: {"max_output_tokens": 20000}`. This is a first-line pragma for the outer `exec` call, not an argument to the nested `js` tool. Keep the exact `nodeRepl.write(await <browser>.documentation());` call shown in the applicable selection scenario below and forward its complete result.

Initialize the runtime once per fresh Node session. If `agent.browsers` already exists, reuse it; do not import or initialize another browser runtime.

```js
if (globalThis.agent?.browsers == null) {
  const { setupBrowserRuntime } = await import("<plugin root>/scripts/browser-client.mjs");
  globalThis.agent = await setupBrowserRuntime();
}
```

Once a browser connection is established, reuse its existing browser binding across later turns and do not reread this skill. Once you have read a browser's complete documentation, do not read it again unless you select a different browser.

A tab binding is separate from its browser binding. If a later turn reports that a tab is missing, stale, closed, or not part of the current browser session, discard that tab binding and obtain or create a fresh tab from the existing browser binding. An empty `browser.tabs.list()` or `browser.user.openTabs()` result is normal after tab cleanup and does not invalidate the browser binding. Never call `agent.browsers.get*` to recover a tab; only an explicit browser-disconnected error invalidates the binding.

## Browser selection
The scenarios below are for the initial browser selection only. Before calling any `agent.browsers.get*` method, reuse an existing `globalThis.browser`, `globalThis.iab`, `globalThis.chrome`, or `globalThis.edge` binding that already serves the task. A new user turn does not invalidate a browser binding or require another selection or documentation call.

Select the initial browser with exactly one of these scenarios, in the order
shown. An explicit request for the in-app browser, Chrome, or Edge always wins
over URL selection. Never call `getForUrl()` when the user names a browser.
An explicit browser request is a hard constraint: use only that browser and
never fall back to another browser surface. If its exact selector is
unavailable, report that browser as unavailable instead of calling
`getDefault()`, `getForUrl()`, or `get("extension")`.

App-provided in-app-browser context is ambient UI state, not a user instruction to select or switch browsers. Only the text of the user's request can explicitly choose a browser.

Do not inspect browser cookies, local storage, profiles, passwords, or session stores. Browser discovery must remain read-only.

When authentication blocks requested browser navigation, do not replace it with web search, a search engine, another site, or another source merely to bypass sign-in.

### The user explicitly requests a browser
A plugin mention in the user's request explicitly names its browser.
`[@Browser](plugin://browser@openai-bundled)` names the in-app browser.
Browser plugin mentions whose URL contains `browserFamily=chrome` or
`browserFamily=edge` name Chrome or Edge respectively.
`[@Chrome](plugin://chrome@openai-bundled)`,
`[@chrome-internal](plugin://chrome-internal@openai-bundled)`, and
`[@chrome-dev](plugin://chrome-dev@openai-bundled)` name Chrome. Follow the
corresponding explicit-browser scenario below.

The in-app browser is available only when the Browser skill is listed for the session. If the user explicitly requests the in-app browser and that skill is available, use a distinct persistent binding and immediately read its complete documentation:

```js
if (globalThis.iab == null) {
  globalThis.iab = await agent.browsers.get("iab");
  nodeRepl.write(await iab.documentation());
}
```

If the user explicitly requests the in-app browser but the Browser skill is not available, report that the in-app browser is unavailable instead of substituting another browser.

Chrome or Edge is available only when a Browser or Chrome skill is listed for
the session and `agent.browsers.get("chrome")` or
`agent.browsers.get("edge")` succeeds. The browser family is a stable selector;
do not list browsers first or pass an opaque browser ID for an explicit family.

For Chrome, use a separate persistent binding and immediately read its complete
documentation:

```js
if (globalThis.chrome == null) {
  globalThis.chrome = await agent.browsers.get("chrome");
  nodeRepl.write(await chrome.documentation());
}
```

For Edge, use its own persistent binding and immediately read its complete
documentation:

```js
if (globalThis.edge == null) {
  globalThis.edge = await agent.browsers.get("edge");
  nodeRepl.write(await edge.documentation());
}
```

If the user explicitly requests Chrome or Edge but that family is unavailable,
tell them that browser needs the ChatGPT browser extension and direct them to
**Settings → Computer use** to install it. Do not substitute another browser.

An explicit browser choice remains in force for the task. If authentication blocks the task in an explicitly selected browser, your next response must explicitly ask the user to sign in in that browser and tell you when it is ready, unless that browser's documentation provides a supported authentication flow to try first. Merely reporting that sign-in is required is not sufficient. Do not switch to another browser unless the user asks or approves the switch.

### The user explicitly requests an external browser without naming a family
When the user says to use their external browser, browser extension, or a
similar external-browser surface without naming Chrome or Edge, select the
first connected extension instance directly. Do not call
`agent.browsers.list()` first:

```js
if (globalThis.browser == null) {
  globalThis.browser = await agent.browsers.get("extension");
  nodeRepl.write(await browser.documentation());
}
```

and the only done-oracle—the authoritative aggregate `snapback verify` receipt (acceptance evidence, not formal proof). `npm test`: raw acceptance implementation that `prove` wraps (debugging). `bun run test:static`: no-server source/generated coherence. `bun run carry:headless`, `bun run carry:web-browser`, `bun run carry:native-simulator`: observation artifacts after accepting the `prove` receipt, never proof authority. `bun run carry:self-check` checks carrier wiring only. Migration: `test:live` was removed; use `npm test` for the same raw acceptance command. ## Extending or ejecting acceptance Keep journey intent and product assertions in `acceptance.mjs`. Extend the journey with generated-operation path tokens plus `step`, `until`, and `defer`. # `@expo/snapback-expo`

The Expo projection for a generated Snapback application. The common path is:

```tsx
import { SnapbackExpoProvider } from '@expo/snapback-expo';
import { app } from './snapback/generated/app';

export default function Root() {
  return <SnapbackExpoProvider app={app}>{/* routes */}</SnapbackExpoProvider>;
}
```

Add `"@expo/snapback-expo"` to `expo.plugins`. The plugin validates the
generated `snapback.app.v1` descriptor and package tuple, registers the
AppState lifecycle shell and the picker-URI asset adapter, and emits a public integration receipt under
`expo.extra.snapback.integrationReceipt`.

The provider registers the adapter once on the existing React/client owner.
Import `useSnapbackActivityPresence` from this facade for typing indicators and
similar intent-scoped presence. It gates foreground admission and adds
background withdrawal to the canonical React hook while sharing the provider's
exact AppState-compatible lifecycle source.

Pass an `expo-image-picker` asset directly to a generated command; the adapter
uses `expo/fetch` to read `content://`, `ph://`, or `file://` into an immutable,
slice-readable structural Blob source that the ordinary asset task already
accepts. Expo's `File` reader handles the narrow Android ImagePicker-cache
case where `expo/fetch` returns a genuine 404. The provider registers the same
WinterCG fetch implementation on the existing asset client for binary TUS
bodies:

```tsx
const picked = result.canceled ? null : result.assets[0];
if (picked) {
  const task = chat.commands.send({ body: 'From Expo', image: picked });
  const outcome = await task.done;
  // outcome.kind: committed | failed | ambiguous | cancelled
}
```

This live-process bridge is transient. It does not claim background upload,
restart recovery, offline source custody, or attempt-grant behavior.

In development, `snapback dev --expo` starts the backend and local Expo/Metro
arms. It injects only a credential-free, loopback rendezvous origin; the
default `SnapbackExpoEnvironmentV1` fetches the expiring supervised binding and
ordinary session from that transient exchange at runtime. No URL prop is
required. A project must already be settled in Sessions auth mode or boot
reports `authority-required` with the native mint refusal.

Release target selection and attestation verification belong to E3. Neither
the `AppBinding` nor the integration receipt carries session authority.

## Documentation outside a checkout

A running Snapback server serves the Guide compiled into that exact build.
These links use the first default development port; use the origin printed by
`snapback dev` or `snapback start` if yours differs.

- Read [the React and Expo client guide](http://127.0.0.1:4287/_snapback/guide/clients/react-expo.md).
- Read first: [the start packets](http://127.0.0.1:4287/_snapback/guide/start/index.md)
  — the budgeted per-template first read (LLP 0259).
- Look up (do not linear-read) the [capability index](http://127.0.0.1:4287/_snapback/guide/capabilities.md).
- Run `snapback guide` or `snapback guide <query>` to browse or search the embedded Guide.
- Run `snapback mcp` for the same build-bound corpus as read-only MCP resources, starting at `snapback-guide://manifest`.

+# Clique build diary
+
+## M1 — identity and profiles
+
+I built password signup/sign-in, generated-principal profile ownership, unique email and handle enforcement, durable browser session custody, logout, profile editing, and fixture-avatar persistence. The first starter segment was replayed twice through the same generated mutations the app uses, with fixture mutation identities retained and transport identities isolated per replay. The M1 suite passed all seven required assertions, the frozen two-client choreography passed all three required checks, and an iOS Hermes bundle was exported.
+
+The easiest part was the explicit data model. Deriving every profile from `ctx.auth.userId` made ownership legible, and the generated references made the frontend/backend seam difficult to mistype. Live profile propagation also worked without special synchronization logic once the query and mutation contracts were correct.
+
+The fight was application boot, not product behavior. A separately launched Metro process had no AppBinding delivery. The combined Expo supervisor then selected several unbounded internal ports, conflicting with the lane's fixed-port constraint, and its custom command health check correctly noticed that Metro was not on the port it had assigned. The eventual fixed-port solution uses the generated descriptor in an explicit provider environment while the backend and Metro stay on 42000 and 42001. Once booted, the untouched M1 choreography went green immediately.
+
+The explicit profile saved time in authorization reasoning and schema review. It cost verbosity: nine tables, twenty-one generated operations, and deliberate function-level read/write/refusal declarations for what would be a few loose handlers elsewhere. That cost felt useful for principal-bound profile state; the code generator caught a guest/profile classification mistake early.
+
+The missing diagnostic was a documented, supported way to run supervised Expo web on caller-selected fixed ports. CLI help exposes the backend port but not the Metro public/process or bootstrap ports. The provider type also accepts an explicit binding override, while the default supervised environment does not consume that override; the necessary custom environment pairing was discoverable only from shipped type and implementation files, not the served Guide.
*** End Patch";

+
+## M2 — feed, graph, posts, and threads
+
+I built Following and Global projections; text, two-image, and video post storage and rendering; URL linkification without unfurling; follow/unfollow, like/unlike, and repost/unrepost set-state mutations; attributed repost feed entries; direct replies and chronological thread screens; and bounded feed paging. The suite passed all twenty-two required assertions. The choreography passed all seven required realtime checks, while retaining the harness's two honest optional skips for image/video composition because the frozen contract has no media-picker control. +
+Creating posts and making likes/reposts live was pleasantly direct. The explicit tables made idempotency obvious: unique pairs plus set-state handlers meant a retry never had to infer intent from the current UI. The live query invalidation path also propagated counts and new feed entries with no client cache surgery.
+
+Navigation fought harder than data. The first browser run showed that the choreography expects feed tabs to remain reachable after its direct profile route and that stacked Expo Router screens can keep background test IDs mounted. I added a lane-owned profile shell around the unchanged frozen ProfileForm and exposed the unchanged frozen FeedTabs there; I also unmounted the background feed composer whenever its screen lost focus. A second loop exposed the harness's display-name extraction assumption—the first text inside `sm-profile`—which the frozen ProfileForm itself does not guarantee because its Edit button precedes the name. The shell now provides a stable name heading without changing the component contract.

+The explicit backend saved time in projection correctness. `feed` declares every read table and the graph edge remains separate from implicit self-membership, so own originals and own reposts could be included without polluting follower counts. The cost was query verbosity and N+1 codegen advisories around projected authors and interactions. For this fixture volume the bounded implementation is correct, but production scale would justify batched exact lookups.

+What was missing was a diagnostic connecting a strict Playwright locator collision to an unfocused Expo Router screen still mounted beneath the thread. The harness receipt was precise enough to infer it, but a route/state snapshot on failure would have shortened the loop. The choreography/profile text-order assumption is also stricter than the frozen ProfileForm's documented contract and would benefit from a dedicated display-name test ID.
